extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists interested in interactive theorem proving, formal verification, and the Lean theorem prover (researchers, developers, and advanced users)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and desiderata for using and designing interactive theorem provers (with a focus on Lean) to verify mathematics and computations: covers logical foundations, system features, metaprogramming, automation, and usability goals. Intended to inform the development and use of proof assistants for verified mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive assertion languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing expressive assertion languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dependent type theory, with type classes, carefully designed abstractions, an equation compiler, and nice syntax to give the user an expressive way to state properties and assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful proof languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing powerful proof languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide both proof terms and tactic-based proof languages, and support custom automation so users can write, structure, and manage large formal proofs effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifying computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify computations step by step for the highest degree of trust; where needed, extract verified code for performance. The system should let users reason about results of computation within a precise formal semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use native implementations for performance but expose internals and use metaprogramming for flexibility (described as “whitebox automation”), enabling powerful automatic or semi-automatic proof steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: User interfaces and tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing better user interfaces and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make everything extensible (automation, parser, debugger, etc.), provide editor/server support with proof-checking and live information, and supply online documentation and courseware to improve usability and adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof object extractability and independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Working with a proof assistant, users construct a formal axiomatic proof; in most systems this proof object can be extracted and verified independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems should produce explicit proof objects (proof terms) that can be checked by independent type checkers or kernels to maximize trust in results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of interactive and automated reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring interactive and automated reasoning together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build an interactive theorem prover with powerful automation and an automated reasoning tool that produces detailed proofs, supports interactive use, has a rich language, and is built on a verified mathematical library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce detailed, checkable proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: An automated reasoning tool should produce (detailed) proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated tools should output detailed proofs that can be inspected and checked in the interactive environment or by independent checkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich formal language
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should have a rich language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support expressive type/language features (dependent types, inductive types, quotients, etc.) so users can formalize varied mathematical concepts naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verified mathematical library
rubrics_metrics.description: Built on a verified mathematical library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide extensive, reusable libraries (analysis, algebra, topology, probability, finite group theory, etc.) so formal developments can rely on verified, well-structured foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise formal semantics for computation
rubrics_metrics.description: A programming environment in which one can compute with objects with a precise formal semantics and reason about the results of computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational features should have a clear formal semantics so computations carried out inside the system are meaningful and suitable for verification and extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small trusted kernel / independent type checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Small trusted kernel with independent type checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the trusted computing base small and provide independent type checking to minimize trust assumptions and facilitate independent verification of proofs and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for constructive and classical reasoning and extensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Supports constructive reasoning, quotients and extensionality, and classical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanisms/axioms (e.g., quotient types implying function extensionality, propositional extensionality, and controlled classical axioms) so both constructive and classical developments are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-integrated type class inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Type class resolution is well integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a robust type-class system and inference mechanism to support algebraic hierarchies and concise, reusable formalizations (examples: semigroup, monoid classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation compiler and flexible function definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: An equation compiler supporting pattern matching, arbitrary structural recursion, nested and mutual inductive definitions, well-founded recursion, and detection of impossible cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a system that compiles high-level function and inductive definitions down to primitives, handles common recursion and pattern-matching idioms, and detects impossible or ill-formed cases to aid definitional clarity and correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible proof styles (term and tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs can be written as terms, or using tactics; support declarative proofs and tactic-style proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow multiple proof styles (proof terms, tactic scripts, structured/Isar-like proofs) so users can choose the most suitable style for clarity, maintainability, or automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/server support and interactive feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Server support for editors, with proof-checking and live information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide language-server-style support (Emacs, VSCode, browser JS frontend) to give immediate feedback, live goal info, and better interactive development workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaprogramming in the object language
rubrics_metrics.description: Go meta and use the object language for metaprogramming; expose the entire library and infrastructure to users writing tactics and automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include: no new language to learn, full access to the library, use of the same debugger/profiler, and the ability to develop theories and automation side-by-side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection API: tactic_state and expr, tactic monad
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose reflection primitives (e.g., tactic_state, expr) and operations acting on them, and provide a tactic monad for imperative-style metaprogramming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark meta definitions clearly, reflect syntax for quotation and pattern matching, and bind VM-level operations to meta constants so metaprograms can manipulate goals and the environment effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel-checked soundness for metaprograms and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics and metaprograms may fail or produce ill-typed expressions, but every object is checked by the kernel before being added to the environment so soundness is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the system so metaprogramming flexibility does not compromise foundational soundness; rely on kernel checks as the last line of defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for automation frameworks and integrated provers
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide built-in and extensible automation frameworks (simplifier with conditional rewriting, arithmetic simplification, SMT-state with congruence closure and e-matching, superposition provers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate a variety of automation tactics and the ability to plug-in or implement new theorem provers and decision procedures to handle common proof obligations automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-performance evaluation and tooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast bytecode interpreter, native numeric representations, native arrays, eager evaluation with thunk support, profiler and debugger; compilation to native code under development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance features let users run large computations inside the system efficiently; profiling and debugging tools aid development of both proofs and metaprograms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensibility and installable tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: An extensible way to declare attributes, assign them to environment objects, and to install tactics written in the language for interactive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow users to extend the environment, register automation, cache results, and integrate user-defined tactics seamlessly into the interactive workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability and broad applicability goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Overarching goals: verify hardware, software, and hybrid systems; verify mathematics; support reasoning and exploration; support formal methods in education; create an eminently powerful, usable system; bring formal methods to the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design priorities should include generality across application domains, pedagogical support, and a focus on usability to encourage widespread adoption.
